blocks.h2: Coolant and oil decide when kit retires
blocks.html:
Machine-shop garments don't wear out — they saturate. Cutting coolant and way oil accumulate in coveralls and trousers until washing stops recovering them, and an oil-loaded garment is both unpleasant and a skin-contact issue. Two habits fix it: rotate enough sets that each garment gets washed hot before oil sets (the oil-and-grease routine), and treat visible saturation as retirement, not character.

The glove question in precision work runs opposite to instinct: near rotating spindles many shops prohibit gloves (entanglement beats laceration as the risk), while handling finished sheet and swarf demands cut level B–D. The task card, not habit, decides — which is exactly how the corridor's aerospace customers audit it.

blocks.h2: The chilled/frozen boundary is a spec boundary
blocks.html:
Chilled work (roughly 0–5 °C) and frozen work (−18 °C and below) look adjacent on the thermometer and are nothing alike on the body. Chilled sections are handled with layering — thermal base, fleece mid, moving in and out freely. Frozen chambers need certified cold-store clothing: EN 342-rated suits whose insulation values are measured, boots with CI (cold-insulated) soles, and — the part sites underplan — work-rest cycles and drying arrangements, because a damp garment insulates like a wet newspaper. A freezer picker in chilled-section kit isn't tough; they're at risk, and the productivity numbers show it before the health ones do.

Everything else in town follows the logistics playbook — with the local note that DIRFT's rail interface puts some roles under railway-adjacent rules their employer will specify.

faq.a: Chilled sections (around 0–5 °C) are managed with layering: thermal base, insulating mid, standard outer. Frozen chambers (−18 °C and below) need certified EN 342 clothing with measured insulation values and cold-rated footwear. The boundary is a specification change, not a thicker jumper.

blocks.h2: Gloves are chosen by chemistry, not toughness
blocks.html:
The EN 388 numbers that dominate glove-buying everywhere else take second place here: against caustic, acids and solvents, what matters is the glove material's resistance to the specific chemical — nitrile for many solvents and oils, butyl against strong acids and ketones, neoprene as the broad-spectrum compromise — and the breakthrough time the manufacturer publishes per substance. A cut-level-D glove in the wrong polymer dissolves into the hazard it was bought to stop. Site COSHH assessments name the products; match the glove chart to the name.

Garment-side, the corridor follows the process-industry layering rule — FR base, type 6 splash over it where permits list exposure — with disposable chemical suits for cleaning and turnaround work, consumed by the case and never re-worn.

faq.q: What gloves protect against caustic soda?
faq.a: Chemical-resistant gloves in a polymer rated for alkalis — nitrile performs well against caustic solutions, with butyl for the strongest exposures — selected on the manufacturer's permeation data for the actual concentration, not on cut ratings. The site COSHH assessment names the product; the glove chart answers it.

faq.q: What does type 6 chemical protection mean?
faq.a: EN 13034 type 6 covers limited liquid splash — mists and light spray, the everyday exposure on process plants — usually as a layer over FR base kit. Higher exposure levels (spray, jets, immersion) move into type 4, 3 and below, which are different garments entirely.

Port kit fails differently: the North Sea's salt spray and near-constant wind fade fluorescent fabric and corrode fittings faster than inland wear ever would, and hi-vis that has quietly dropped below its class is the most dangerous garment on the quay because everyone still trusts it. The discipline is scheduled inspection — colour and tape checks on a calendar, not on a feeling — and buying garments whose zips and poppers are plastic or coated rather than bare metal.

The other local reality is shift weather: a 2am winter gate shift and a July afternoon on the same roster. That argues for the layering logic in our jacket guide — waterproof shell sized over insulating layers that come and go — rather than one garment asked to do every season.

blocks.h2: Two eras of steel, one gate

While hot metal runs, nothing about the classic spec relaxes: EN ISO 11612 with code E molten-iron performance, radiant-heat capability, heavy shed-splash fabrics and HRO-soled boots (the codes) stay the price of entry to the hot end. The arc-furnace era shifts the emphasis rather than erasing it — molten steel is still molten steel — but adds a serious electrical dimension: high-power switching and furnace electrics put arc-rated clothing on lists where it never appeared before.

And through the build years, the works is simultaneously a construction site inside an operating plant — meaning contractors carry both the site baseline and whatever hot-zone or electrical spec their permit adds. Buying to the induction document, crew by crew, is the whole game here.
